newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir leader takes office as separatists strike.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader takes office as separatists strike.

text.p: The leader of Kashmir's largest pro-India party took office on Wednesday at the head of the region's first local government since a separatist revolt broke out nearly seven years ago.

Under tight security, National Conference chairman Farooq Abdullah was sworn in as chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state in a ceremony in Srinagar, the state's summer capital and the focus of the separatist insurgency.
Shops, businesses and schools in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir valley were shut after separatists opposed to the new government called for a strike throughout the Himalayan region.
Last week Abdullah's party won 58 seats in the state's 87-member assembly in the first elections since 1987, scoring an absolute majority and inflicting humiliating defeat on rivals.
With eight seats, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party lagged far behind.

Dozens of separatist groups fighting for independence or closer ties to neighbouring Pakistan have rejected Abdullah's government. They boycotted the polls, which they called a mockery of Kashmiri aspirations.
Kashmir's leading separatist coalition, the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, a combine of about 30 political parties, called on Kashmiris to observe a "Black Day" on Wednesday.
"Both Azad Kashmir as well as Indian-occupied Kashmir will observe October 9 as a Black Day," Hurriyat leader Gulam Nabi Sumji said in a statement.

Pakistan rules one third of the disputed region, called Azad (Free) Kashmir, while India holds the rest. The two nations have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947.
Except for police and security patrols, the streets of Srinagar were deserted on Wednesday.
A police spokesman told Reuters security had been beefed up in Srinagar, especially around the conference hall on Dal Lake where Abdullah's government took the oath of office.

Senior Indian politicians from a range of parties attended the ceremony, closing ranks with Abdullah despite political differences to present a united face for the Himalayan region in the face of the separatist movement.
Former prime minister V.P. Singh and Congress party president Sitaram Kesri attended the oath-taking.
Abdullah contested the polls on a promise of autonomy for the region, which includes Hindu-dominated Jammu, predominantly Moslem Kashmir and Buddhist Ladakh.
But his first tasks were to reconcile the separatists and put the battered economy back on track.
Earlier Abdullah said he was unperturbed by the Hurriyat's strike call. "They (Hurriyat) have been always calling strikes and this is not going to affect us," he said earlier this week.
The Hurriyat has rejected Abdullah's offer for talks, but the politician has kept the door open to negotiations.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed in the revolt. Both Abdullah and the Hurriyat put the figure at some 50,000.
India accuses Islamabad of funding and arming the separatist guerrillas in the region. Pakistan denies the charges, saying its role is limited to political and diplomatic support.
